articles.title: Socialism's growing appeal meets an awkward reality check on college campus
articles.summary: University of Michigan students offered over a dozen different definitions of socialism, reflecting a national confusion highlighted by Gallup polling.
articles.body: ANN ARBOR, Mich. — Socialism is gaining popularity among young Americans, but Fox News Digital found strikingly different understandings of the ideology among college students, some of whom acknowledged that their generation may not fully grasp what they're embracing. A recent Fox News poll found that 48% of Americans ages 18 to 34 viewed socialism favorably, compared with 32% of Americans overall. When Fox News Digital asked more than a dozen University of Michigan students to define socialism, their answers ranged from government-funded safety nets and affordable health care to collective ownership of industry. "If the definition was more widely known, people would support it less honestly," one student, Ahnika, told Fox News Digital. Other students acknowledged the confusion, while at least a dozen declined to be interviewed on camera because they said they did not know enough about socialism to give an informed answer. THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM "Absolutely. I feel like many people don't really understand, I feel, the full grasp or scope of what socialism really means," a student named Owen told Fox News Digital. "I think they kind of have a more idealistic image of it." The divide over what socialism actually means comes as the ideology becomes an increasingly prominent issue in American politics, including Michigan's closely watched Senate contest, where Republicans have sought to tie Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed to socialism – despite his rejection of the label. Socialism? It's a safety net Some of the students interviewed used the word socialism as a way to describe a government that spends more money on subsidizing healthcare, housing or other basic necessities. "It's an economic system in which the resources of the government … are allocated into public services such as housing, affordable housing, food like food banks, education, things like that," James, one student, told Fox News Digital. "Socialism to me is a concept in politics where everybody gets a little bit of everything. Everybody benefits and everybody is really taken care of. Kind of that social net that you see in other types of politics," Kayla, another student, said. "It's a political system where less social goods are delivered by the market than in capitalism," said her fellow student, Sam. Republicans and centrist Democrats have both raised concerns about the rising tide of socialism, while young people turn to it as a solution to the cost of living. "Does the socialism thing scare me? Yes. Is it the wrong solution? Yes," Vice President JD Vance said in a July interview. "But one thing I try to persuade my fellow Republicans of is socialism is the alternative if we don’t have a pathway to give people a sense that the system is not rigged and that the American dream is attainable." While the precise definition of socialism is debated by economists and philosophers, the ideology generally calls for replacing private ownership of major productive assets with some form of public, collective or worker ownership, though socialists differ sharply over whether that control should be exercised through the government, workers themselves or other institutions. Modern socialism emerged as a major political and economic movement in 19th-century Europe, fueled by concerns over wealth inequality, industrial working conditions and the concentration of economic power in private hands. A fair number of the students who spoke with Fox News Digital had understandings of socialism more in line with this traditional definition. EL-SAYED REVEALS HE WOULD GO ‘STEP FURTHER’ THAN SANDERS ON SOCIALIST PLAN FOR MAJOR US INDUSTRY Or is it government control? "It's an economic system where certain aspects [of the economy] are controlled by the government such as health care, possibly housing, agriculture, general necessities," Owen said. "It's distinct from communism in that the government does not have free rein over every aspect of the market, but it's not the same as capitalism where the free market determines everything." How far government control should extend has long divided socialists. Some advocate government ownership of nearly all major industries, while others favor worker-owned businesses amid a mix of public and private enterprise. "I guess I would define it as an economic system where resources are shared in a more, in a somewhat equitable sense, and there's some level of, you know, public control of that," Zack, also a student at the university, told Fox News Digital. "It’s not really any more specific than that, socialism is a broad term, you know?" While some young Americans associate socialism with government control of private businesses, an idea that has long faced resistance in American politics, the ideology has gained support among younger voters, even as they differ over what it would mean in practice. The Democratic Socialists of America, which advocates replacing capitalism with a more collectively controlled economy, has seen its ranks swell with members and notched a series of electoral victories during the second Trump administration. "I'd say I define socialism by the government taking collective ownership of companies’ production and distribution of goods," student Ahnika told Fox News Digital. "As far as I’m aware, it’s about like workers and members of society owning the product … as opposed to capitalism where you make the product, if you work on an assembly line, the product goes to your manager or whoever runs the factory and then they make most of the profit off of your work," Noah, also a student, told Fox News Digital. Maybe it's Canada? Others defined socialism in relation to countries or politicians. "Mostly I think of Canada when I think of socialism," Samantha, another student, told Fox News Digital. Elyse, her peer, said that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani comes to mind when thinking of a definition for socialism. LIBERAL-CITY RESIDENT HESITATES WHEN PRESSED ON BELIEFS: 'I HADN'T REALLY THOUGHT ABOUT SOCIALISM THAT WAY' The University of Michigan’s student body isn’t alone in its division over the definition of socialism. Gallup found in 2018 that 23% of Americans thought the word meant "equality, including equal rights, standing or distribution," while 10% defined it as "provision of benefits and services, such as health care," 6% said it was "communism or a modified version of it" and further 6% understood it to be "being social or getting along with others." Roughly a quarter of respondents had no opinion on the definition of socialism, and just 17% described it as "government ownership or control of businesses and the economy," the definition typically favored by economists. Michigan, where many of the students interviewed vote, could easily decide control of Congress following November’s midterm elections. Socialism is a major issue in the race, with Republicans attempting to portray Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as a socialist — a label he rejects despite a long-running association with the Democratic Socialists of America. At least a dozen students told Fox News Digital that they were not comfortable filming an interview because they did not feel they knew enough about socialism to give an informed response, further highlighting the degree of confusion surrounding the term among young people. LIBERAL HOT SPOT RESIDENTS CAN’T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS AS FAR-LEFT MOVEMENTS GAINS STEAM While the students couldn’t agree on what socialism meant, they did agree that their peers were confused. "Yeah, I mean there's sort of a general idea of an equitable distribution of resources, but other than that, in terms of how it should be done, um like what it actually looks like, how power is distributed, there's a lot of open questions there," said Zach. "Yeah, absolutely. There's a huge misconception about socialism, even capitalism as well," a student named Jeff told Fox News Digital. "So I think these terms in the broader space of political thought are probably allegories depending on your political orientation for good or bad … that's probably the most ubiquitous use of that term. ‘Socialism bad, capitalism good,’ or vice versa if you're a progressive." THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS Other students felt their peers were too quick to define socialism in relation to other political systems. "I would say some people would compare socialism to communism as being practically identical, whereas others would just understand it as having a stronger social safety net like in like Nordic countries," Sam said, noting that he doesn’t feel there is a right or wrong definition for the word. "Yeah, I feel like a lot of people don't really understand what socialism is," Tommy, another student, said. "I feel like they think that sometimes it's communism and they conflate the two. So I feel like people need to educate themselves on what the concept actually is." One student felt that, if more people understood socialism to imply government ownership of industry, the system would be significantly less popular. "I honestly think there’s a bit of confusion … If the definition was more widely known, people would support it less honestly," Ahnika said. "Rather than having a good understanding of what socialism is, people often try to antagonize the opposite end of the spectrum, which is private ownership." Not everyone felt that the ambiguity surrounding the term was necessarily a bad thing, however. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think having complex definitions of things only encourages conversation and when those conversations can be productive and when we approach them in a productive way I think we only uh strengthen what can be the collective definition of stuff like socialism," Elyse told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump announces new Audi factory at Georgia campaign rally
articles.summary: President Trump announced a new Audi factory while campaigning in Georgia on Saturday, a move that arrived almost a week before November’s midterms. “Today, I’m thrilled to announce a massive auto manufacturing investment in the great state of Georgia by a fantastic company,” Trump said during the Saturday rally. “Audi has just committed to invest…
articles.body:
President Trump announced a new Audi factory while campaigning in Georgia on Saturday, a move that arrived almost a week before November’s midterms.

“Today, I’m thrilled to announce a massive auto manufacturing investment in the great state of Georgia by a fantastic company,” Trump said during the Saturday rally.

“Audi has just committed to invest $4.2 billion in nearby Macon, Georgia, to begin the construction next month on a massive plant that will produce 200,000 cars a year. Think of that, think of that. Two hundred thousand cars a year, that’s incredible,” he added.

In a Saturday press release, Audi said that the company “is taking a major step in its global growth strategy with plans to establish its first U.S. plant site in Georgia, which will be among one of the brand’s largest production footprints globally.”

The company said in its release that the plant’s construction will start next year .

“Audi is building its future in America. As part of our larger U.S. strategy, we are focused on becoming an even more significant player in this market,” Audi of America’s president, Vito Paladino said in the release.

“This investment signifies the brand’s commitment to our customers, dealers, employees, and communities across the country.”

Trump’s announcement comes shortly before the midterms next month, in which he and his party are facing concerns over the U.S. economy due to the effects of the war against Iran and his tariffs.

The president’s approval rating has also slumped as of late, with it sitting at 39.1 percent on Sunday morning and his disapproval at 59.5 percent, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ.

articles.title: America the Beautiful Act honors Theodore Roosevelt’s conservation legacy
articles.summary: The bipartisan America the Beautiful Act, which proposes an international visitor surcharge to fund the maintenance of national parks and public lands, is moving through Congress.
articles.body:
Theodore Roosevelt always went big. That was especially so with our national landscape. He left America a remarkable conservation inheritance. During his presidency, he protected some 230 million acres of public land — roughly one-third of all federal land that exists today — and helped establish conservation as an enduring American ideal.

More than a century later, honoring that legacy requires more than protecting land. It requires taking care of what we already have.

That is the promise of the America the Beautiful Act , bipartisan legislation currently making its way through Congress that offers a smarter path for funding the stewardship of America’s national parks and public lands. The act dedicates resources to the upkeep of what we already own, making those dollars work harder, and asks international visitors to contribute more toward the care of the extraordinary places they travel here to enjoy.

National parks may be, in the words of Wallace Stegner, America’s best idea , but behind the postcard views lies a massive $24 billion maintenance challenge . Roads and bridges need repair. Trails and campgrounds are deteriorating. Water systems, visitor facilities and historic structures are aging.

These problems lack the romance of creating a new national park, but conservation at its core is about taking care of what you own.

A rancher who buys more land while letting his fences fall down isn’t practicing good stewardship. Neither is a government that lets the public’s lands fall into disrepair.

The America the Beautiful Act recognizes that distinction.

The legislation would secure up to $1.9 billion a year for the Legacy Restoration Fund through 2031, dedicating significant resources to deferred maintenance across national parks and other public lands. It would prioritize projects that address safety risks and high visitation impacts, prevent assets from deteriorating into more expensive problems, and make measurable progress against maintenance backlogs.

Just as importantly, those dollars will continue to be dedicated to caring for what we already own, rather than acquiring additional lands. Conservation isn’t measured simply in acres. It is also measured by the condition in which we leave those acres to the next generation.

Critically, the bill contains an innovative way to help pay for that work: an international visitor surcharge at national parks.

The Interior Department has already taken a first step in this direction. Beginning this year, it imposed an additional $100 charge on international visitors at 11 of the nation’s busiest parks. The America the Beautiful Act would put the concept into law and expand it to National Park System units that charge entrance fees, with the additional revenue supporting deferred maintenance.

It’s an idea the Property and Environment Research Center has championed for years and presented to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in 2025.

The market logic is simple: International tourists often spend thousands of dollars traveling to see Yellowstone, Yosemite or the Grand Canyon. Park admission fees represent a tiny fraction of their trip. Asking them to pay a bit more means every dollar they contribute is a dollar American taxpayers don’t have to.

Other countries already use similar pricing at prized natural and cultural attractions, like the Louvre in Paris, France, or the Galapagos Islands in Ecuador, so why not try this approach at home?

It is a virtuous conservation loop. People value a place enough to visit it, their visit generates revenue, and that revenue helps keep America’s parks beautiful. In other words, conservation can help pay for conservation.

This approach would have been familiar to Theodore Roosevelt. His conservation ethic was grounded not simply in preservation, but in stewardship — the responsibility to use America’s natural wealth wisely and leave it in good condition for those who come after us. Theodore Roosevelt learned this as a rancher in the Dakotas before becoming president. When he and George Bird Grinnell founded the Boone and Crockett Club, in 1887, its first task was securing the wildlife and resources of Yellowstone, then a park in name only. Protecting a place was the beginning of the work, not the end of it. Fittingly, the bill has a champion in Burgum, who led the state where Roosevelt’s conservation ethic was forged.

This Oct. 27 marks Theodore Roosevelt’s 168th birthday. What more fitting way to honor his legacy than for Congress to pass this critical piece of legislation immediately after the election and send it to the president’s desk? More than a century after he helped make conservation an American ideal, the occasion is an opportune reminder of what his legacy asks of us. But time is of the essence in the remaining days of this Congress.

Roosevelt helped conserve an extraordinary inheritance. Our job is to take care of it. Now.

Brian Yablonski is the chief executive officer of the Property and Environment Research Center. Simon Roosevelt is the executive vice president of conservation at the Boone and Crockett Club.

The Justice Department (DOJ) reportedly sent letters Friday to California election officials, directing them to identify potential noncitizens on…
articles.body:
With less than two weeks to go before the midterms, the Trump administration is ramping up its warnings about voter fraud and is not ruling out the prospect of weighing in on states’ election certification efforts.

The Justice Department (DOJ) reportedly sent letters Friday to California election officials, directing them to identify potential noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls or “risk significant federal scrutiny.”

There will be an emergency hearing on Sunday at 4 p.m. EDT on whether California must segregate ballots submitted by the 20,000 people who the DOJ says are noncitizens.

The DOJ filed a suit on Thursday to prevent the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) loses in this year’s midterms. President Trump told reporters Friday that he had pushed for the election challenge himself.

Attorney General Todd Blanche appeared on CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday with Dana Bash, where he said that the Alaska Senate race was “not a fair fight.” He is also set to appear on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

Meanwhile, Trump is starting his Sunday in Mar-a-Lago but will head to Port Huron, Mich., for a 2 p.m. rally. The Senate race in the state between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed has been tightening. The president has ramped up his rally appearances in GOP states ahead of November’s midterms.

articles.body:
President Trump went after Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Alaska’s ranked choice voting system on Saturday.

“The Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far, Lisa Murkowski, of the Great State of Alaska (A State for which I produced, on a continuing basis, Billions and Billions of Dollars, and which Crooked Joe Biden and the Dumocrats had totally shut down —” Trump said in a late-night Truth Social post.

“Then I came back, and delivered even more!), who only got elected because of Corrupt Ranked Choice Voting, is upset because I revealed what everyone knows, that the Ranked Choice Voting Ballot is a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before.”

“Lisa Murkowski is a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country. You just don’t get any worse!” the president added later.

On Friday, Trump said he ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to file a lawsuit to prevent certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) loses in this year’s midterms.

The DOJ filed the suit on Thursday, stating that the existence of a candidate with a close name to Sullivan’s would result in an invalid win for Democrat Mary Peltola. The president told reporters Friday that he had pushed for the election challenge himself.

“I’m the one who said do it,” Trump said.

In response to the suit, Murkowski said in a post on the social platform X on Friday that “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.”

“The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit,” she added.

The issue comes from Daniel J. Sullivan, a separate person from the Senator who is running for the upper chamber in Alaska, who will appear on the November ballot against the incumbent senator.

The top four vote-receiving candidates in Alaska’s primary go on to the general election. The two Sullivans will show up differently on the ballot, with the senator labeled “incumbent” and “Republican.”

articles.title: Hochul faces revolt from unlikely New Yorkers as Democrats deliver scathing verdict on their party
articles.summary: Former Democratic Bronx Assemblyman Stephen Kaufman accuses his own party of being overtaken by socialists while rallying for Bruce Blakeman.
articles.body: BRONX, N.Y. – Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman is courting disaffected Democrats as he seeks to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, betting that frustration over affordability, crime and the party's leftward shift could help him make inroads with traditionally Democratic voters. "They're not Democrats. They're socialists and communists," former Democratic Bronx Assemblyman Stephen Kaufman told Fox News Digital. "They're just not Democrats, they're not moderates." Kaufman delivered the blistering criticism while rallying alongside Blakeman at the Crosstown Diner in the Bronx, where several voters expressed similar frustrations with Democratic leadership and said they were backing the Republican candidate. "Every time I go out and meet the people, another Democrat comes up to me and says, 'Bruce, I'm a lifelong Democrat. I've never voted Republican in my life. We're voting for you,'" Blakeman told Fox News Digital. NY SOCIALIST SURGE COULD PUSH DEM VOTERS TO DEFECT, GOP GOVERNOR CANDIDATE PREDICTS Kaufman accused the Democratic Socialists of America of gaining increasing influence over the party, warning that Democrats are "rapidly becoming a house of hatred" that no longer welcomes moderate voices. Several Bronx voters who spoke with Fox News Digital echoed those concerns, pointing to rising costs, public safety and the Democratic Party's increasingly progressive direction as reasons they feel politically abandoned. "It's not your Democratic Party anymore. It's not your grandfather's Democratic Party. It's become the Democratic Socialist, a.k.a. Communist Party," Lisa, a resident of the Bronx's Throggs Neck neighborhood, said. "The socialists here literally said we’re land-hoarding if we only have a single-family home or a four-family home and that we were a problem… Kathy was all in support and quiet about it. She didn’t defend the homeowners," another man from the Bronx added. BRUCE BLAKEMAN HAMMERS DEM GOV HOCHUL, MAMDANI OVER SUBWAY SAFETY DURING NYC CAMPAIGN RIDE One registered Democrat said the party's failure to address the needs of working families was driving his political decisions. "I'm a registered Democrat. Ask me if I vote that way," he said. "I vote to what affects me, my community, the people I live with. I vote who's going to help the middle class." SHOCK POLL: POWERFUL BLUE STATE GOV'S LEAD SHRINKS TO SINGLE DIGITS WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION Blakeman argued that growing frustration with Hochul's leadership has created an opening for Republicans in a state long dominated by Democrats. "Kathy Hochul has raised taxes. She's raised utility rates 48 times. Programs like cashless bail make it easier for criminals to operate in our neighborhoods. So now I have the evidences. I have her report card and it's straight F's," said Blakeman. Kaufman said that Hochul has embraced and catered towards the further left of her party. THE IRAN WAR DIDN'T MAKE YOUR HEATING BILL THIS HIGH. BLUE-STATE ENERGY POLICY DID "The electricity rates have skyrocketed. She's had 42 increases over time. She wouldn't permit building of gas lines. She's closed utility plants. All she does is move harder and harder to the left. Which don't represent people in this neighborhood," he said. "Every time she has a problem, she goes crying to the hard left. She's totally controlled by them," Kaufman added. Blakeman, meanwhile, told Fox News Digital he would take the opposite approach, pledging to cut taxes and utility bills while making communities safer. "I will cut taxes. I will cut utility bills. And I will make for safer communities just like I did in my own county as county executive," Blakeman said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Blakeman pointed to his record as Nassau County executive, saying he has "not raised taxes a penny in five years" and has instead cut taxes by $150 million. "I’ll take my record, compare it to hers," he said, arguing he would "cut their taxes, cut the utility bills and make safer communities." The socialist wing of the Democratic Party has moved from the margins to positions of real political power, particularly in New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani became mayor and DSA-backed candidates went on to topple Democratic incumbents in congressional primaries. The movement has also scored victories beyond New York, with DSA-backed Melat Kiros defeating longtime Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado and self-described democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George capturing the Democratic mayoral nomination in Washington, D.C. Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's office for comment.

articles.title: Sen. Adam Schiff says Pete Hegseth should testify on Starlink slowdown in Ukraine
articles.summary: Sen. Adam Schiff said that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should testify before the Senate on the Starlink satellite limitations that disrupted Ukrainian military operations.
articles.body: Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., told NBC’s “Meet the Press” Sunday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should testify before the Senate on the Starlink satellite limitations that disrupted Ukrainian military operations. If Democrats retake the Senate, Schiff told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker, “Defense Secretary Hegseth should be brought in. Anyone who has knowledge of what happened.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on “Meet the Press” last week that the Ukrainian government believed the decision to limit Starlink came from the U.S. government. Zelenskyy said at the time that “it was the message from American government to limit this speed, and technically SpaceX did it.” The Wall Street Journal reported last week that President Donald Trump called Musk and asked him to lift his company’s satellite service restrictions. Ukraine said Saturday that Starlink and Starshield, its military network, were working at high speeds again. Last week, the systems were disrupted, and Ukraine said the disruptions made it harder to intercept incoming Russian attacks. “You’ve got the president saying one thing, you’ve got Elon Musk saying another thing, you have them both saying different things at different times,” Schiff said. “Somebody is lying here. Maybe they’re all lying in different ways, but we need to find out.” The disruptions to Starlink, which is run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, led to rising tensions with the U.S. amid questions about who may have ordered the slowdown of the satellite services. Overnight, Musk accused Ukraine in posts to X of violating “Starlink terms of service” by using the system for offensive strikes. He said the “loophole was closed” and said that the company “simply enforced our terms of service when they were bypassed.” Musk previously said that limits on “speed or usage” of Starshield are “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Schiff said Sunday that “the world’s richest person shouldn’t be controlling our national security interests.” “That is a spectacular threat to our national security,” he said. “If it is true, we should find out.” Schiff referenced Musk’s overnight posts about Starlink’s policies, saying that “something changed within the last week.” “What was it that changed?” Schiff said. “Why did it change? What impact is it having on Ukraine’s ability to defend itself? Is this in our national security interests? These are the questions we should ask, which frankly Republicans have been unwilling to ask.” On Thursday, Trump said Musk restored Starlink in Ukraine. One day later, though, Ukraine denied that the satellite system was working properly. The Trump administration has denied that it requested changes to Starlink’s operation in Ukraine. “The reporting out there was that somehow the United States government was denying them something they needed in order to defend their country,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week. “That’s not true. That’s not accurate.”

articles.title: Blanche: Alaska Senate race is ‘not a fair fight’ to Trump
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday said President Trump doesn’t consider Alaska’s Senate race to be a fair contest because of the controversial appearance on the ballot of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), which he argued could confuse voters and potentially cost Republicans the seat. Speaking on CNN’s…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday said President Trump doesn’t consider Alaska’s Senate race to be a fair contest because of the controversial appearance on the ballot of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), which he argued could confuse voters and potentially cost Republicans the seat.

Speaking on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche defended a Justice Department lawsuit aiming to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if the incumbent loses his reelection bid.

“What he has said repeatedly, repeatedly, is that the reason why this is not fair — this is not a fair fight in his mind — is because there is a man on the ballot with the same name as the incumbent senator, who happens to be a Republican,” Blanche said.

Trump on Friday said he directed the DOJ to file the lawsuit, which alleges that the existence of a candidate with a similar name to Sullivan would invalidate a win by opponent Mary Pelota (D).

The department argues that Daniel J. Sullivan is running with the intention of confusing voters and is asking the court to block the certification of the election in a scenario where if all the votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan had instead gone to the incumbent, the incumbent would have won.

“There could be a crime. But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard,” Blanche said.

Despite Trump’s public acknowledgement, Blanche declined to say whether the president had instructed him to pursue the lawsuit when pressed by CNN host Dana Bash, saying he would not disclose their private conversations.

“I will never talk about any communications I have with the president of the United States,” he said. “But what I will say is that the president is not shy to the American people and has been very clear with the American people about his concerns about what’s happening in Alaska.”

Alaska election officials previously sought to disqualify Daniel J. Sullivan over allegations that he entered the race to confuse voters. He was ultimately allowed to remain on the ballot following litigation in state courts.

articles.title: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer says America is ready to elect a woman
articles.summary: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a female president.
articles.body: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a female president. “Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I’ve heard everyone say, ‘You can’t have this person or that person,’” the governor told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “I would put my money on any Democratic governor in the country against [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio in 2028,” she added, pointing to two Republicans widely expected to run for president in two years. Asked directly whether a woman could be the best choice to beat a potential GOP presidential nominee in 2028, Whitmer simply said, “I do.” In 2025, Obama said in public remarks: “As we saw in this past election, sadly, we ain’t ready. That’s why I’m like, don’t even look at me about running, because you all are lying. You’re not ready for a woman. You are not.” Several women, including Whitmer and former Vice President Kamala Harris, are widely speculated to be potential candidates in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. On Sunday, Whitmer did not deny that she’s exploring a potential run for president in 2028, saying that she’ll decide on her next steps after she departs from her post as governor in January. “When I exit office … I’m going to take a little time off and figure out what I want to do next, so I’ve got nothing new to share with you, unfortunately,” Whitmer told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. Earlier this year, Whitmer denied that she planned to run for president but quickly walked back the comments. “There will be a robust group of people running for president,” she said at the time, adding, “I will not be one of them in 2028, I can tell you that.” Later the same day, the governor said: “I never thought I would run for governor. So I guess I should know better to never say never.” Several other Democratic governors, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, are also widely regarded as potential 2028 presidential candidates. Each has been crisscrossing the country ahead of the midterms campaigning on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in competitive races. Whitmer on Sunday highlighted her support for former public health official Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor in Ohio. Earlier this week, Acton’s opponent, GOP businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, released a TV ad featuring Acton’s mother calling her a “liar.” Acton has publicly shared that she’s been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years and has accused her late stepfather of sexually abusing her. Acton and her brother were removed from her mother’s custody in 1978 after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested on a child rape charge. Acton’s mother has not responded to requests for comment. “I’m going to stay focused on getting people like Amy Acton over the finish line. What’s happened to her in Ohio is absolutely abhorrent, and any survivor knows there’s always a backlash. But this is what makes it harder for women to seek help after they’ve been sexually assaulted in this country,” Whitmer said on Sunday. “It is unreal what’s going on, and that’s why we’ve got to — we’ve got to win races like this and elect good people who are going to keep the people at the heart of their work, like Dr. Amy Acton.” Ramaswamy’s decision to air the ad has faced widespread bipartisan condemnation, including from Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who is locked in a tight re-election race.

articles.title: SNAP winners and losers: Which states are facing possible funding cuts?
articles.summary: Time is ticking for states to slash their error rates or risk losing a sizable amount of federal funding for SNAP.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Time is ticking for states to slash their error rates or risk losing a sizable amount of federal funding for SNAP.

The pressure comes from a law passed last year that ties error rates to federal funds for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the program formerly known as Food Stamps.

States need to meet a target error rate under 6% to avoid being impacted, but so far only a small minority have made the cut. As of the 2025 fiscal year , only nine states had error rates under 6% and 41 states were still in trouble.

The error rate refers to the percentage of SNAP benefits paid either above or below what people should have received, primarily because of mistakes. It includes overpayments and underpayments, but overpayments are more common.

The national average error rate is about 11%.

So far, only nine states have met the new 6% goal: Idaho, Iowa, Kentucky, Nebraska, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Everyone else still has some work to do – and some states have a lot of work to do. Alaska has the highest error rate in the country at 23%. If that sounds bad, it’s a big improvement from 2023, when the state’s error rate was 60%.

The state’s error rate is so high, the Department of Health said, because it has been prioritizing keeping food assistance going, even when some documentation was missing. “While this approach helped protect access to food assistance, it increased the risk of procedural and administrative errors,” spokesperson Megan Darrow previously told Anchorage Daily News .

See your state’s SNAP error rate by exploring the map below.

Most states have just one more year to get their acts together. Federal law says states can choose to use either their 2025 or 2026 error rates when determining what percentage of SNAP benefits they must pay starting in October 2027, so last year’s numbers (in the map above) were the first to count.

Error rates are so high in Alaska, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, New Mexico, Oregon and D.C. that they’ll be given at least one more year to try and reduce them.

What happens in states with high error rates?

In states where error rates remain above 6%, the law doesn’t directly cut the benefits SNAP recipients are paid. Instead, it forces states to come up with the funding themselves. States will be forced to shoulder 5% to 15% of benefit costs, depending on how bad their error rate is.

The indirect effect, however, may still end up being that families who rely on SNAP see their monthly allotment go down. As a result of the cost shift, the Congressional Budget Office estimates that some states will end up reducing or eliminating SNAP benefits for about 300,000 people. Subsidies through child nutrition programs could also decrease for about 96,000 children.

Consider Missouri as an example. It had an error rate of 8.7% last year. Unless it improves next year, the state will have to pick up 10% of SNAP benefit costs starting in October 2027.

Missouri residents received about $1.5 billion of SNAP benefits in 2024, the latest year for which federal data is available. If that same amount of benefits is paid in the future, Missouri could have to cover $150 million of the costs; that’s a sum greater than the total budgeted for several state prisons.

As potential funding cuts loom, SNAP aid has already been dropping faster than expected since the 2025 passage of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which tightened up several eligibility requirements.

Data show SNAP enrollment fell from 42.2 million in May 2025 to 36.6 million in May, a drop of more than 13% in a year. The May data are preliminary and could be revised.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump immigration win could strengthen admin's hand in looming Supreme Court fight
articles.summary: The Fifth Circuit Friday ruled illegal immigrants never formally admitted to the U.S. have no constitutional right to individualized bond hearings.
articles.body: The Trump administration scored a major full-panel victory at the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals Friday, which ruled that detained illegal immigrants who were never formally admitted into the U. S. are not constitutionally entitled to bond hearings while awaiting deportation. The ruling comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha this term, a closely related fight over whether the federal mandatory-detention statute applies at all to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country — setting up the possibility that the justices could either undercut Friday’s ruling or strengthen the government's hand. The Fifth Circuit answered the constitutional question in Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez v. Sylvester M. Ortega, finding that three immigrant men detained under the mandatory-detention statute are not entitled to bond hearings under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The court held that their years or even decades of residence in the United States, along with ties to the country and their communities, do not create a constitutional right to a bond hearing. "The Constitution does not entitle them to a bond hearing," the court wrote. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT Meanwhile, the Supreme Court will consider Rhoney, a case out of the Second Circuit, to determine whether the mandatory-detention law applies to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country in the first place. At the center of the issue is a 9-2 circuit split over which federal detention law applies to immigrants who entered the country illegally, were never formally admitted and were later arrested by immigration authorities after living in the U.S. for years — sometimes decades after crossing the border. The Fifth and Eighth Circuits have held that those immigrants remain "applicants for admission" under Section 1225 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, subjecting them to mandatory detention without an ordinary bond hearing while their removal proceedings play out. Nine other federal appeals courts have ruled that Section 1226 applies instead, which provides a path for them to seek release on bond. The Supreme Court will essentially decide whether immigrants who entered illegally and have lived in the U.S. for years can be subjected to the same mandatory-detention provision that applies to certain immigrants seeking admission into the country. If the Supreme Court sides with the Second Circuit, Barbosa da Cunha — a Brazilian national who entered the country illegally roughly two decades ago and was detained in 2025 — would have a path to seek release on bond. Such a ruling would likely apply to the three longtime immigrants at the center of Rodriguez as well, substantially undercutting the significance of Friday’s ruling by eliminating the need to answer the constitutional question of whether due process requires a bond hearing. SUPREME COURT TAKES UP FIGHT OVER TRUMP’S THIRD-COUNTRY ILLEGAL ALIEN DEPORTATION POLICY Judge Leslie Southwick pointed directly to the looming Supreme Court fight in her dissent. Should the Supreme Court eventually determine that this court was wrong as to the statute, then the constitutional issue we address here will have far less significance. It certainly has significance at the moment," Southwick wrote. But conservative legal experts say Rodriguez could also strengthen the administration’s hand in Rhoney by undercutting one argument against the government’s interpretation of Section 1225: that applying the mandatory-detention provision to longtime residents would raise serious constitutional concerns. Michael Morley, a constitutional law professor at Florida State University, said Friday’s ruling could influence how the justices approach that question because courts often consider whether a particular reading of federal law would create constitutional problems. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA "The Fifth Circuit’s en banc ruling in Rodriguez today takes the next step by holding that such detention would not violate the U.S. Constitution’s Due Process Clause," Morley said. "This holding may impact the Supreme Court’s reasoning, because an important consideration in disputes over federal laws is whether a particular interpretation would be unconstitutional." "If the Court agrees with the Fifth Circuit’s analysis that the Due Process Clause allows such detention, it may be more likely to conclude that federal law permits it, as well, Morley continued. Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, argued that the decision could bolster the administration as the justices prepare to resolve the circuit split. "I actually think this ruling will help the government in the Rhoney case," von Spakovsky said, pointing to the Fifth Circuit’s position that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for immigrants who were never admitted to the United States. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "There was already a split in the circuit courts on this issue but the Fifth Circuit has consistently held that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for aliens who were never admitted to the United States," he said. "I will be surprised if a majority of the Supreme Court disagrees when they ultimately issue a decision in the Rhoney case." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled oral arguments in Rhoney, which it agreed to hear earlier this month.

articles.title: CPM seeks CM’s stand on governor’s PSC move
articles.summary: CPM asks Kerala CM to clarify stance on ex-governor Arlekar’s recommendation to dissolve PSC, calling it unconstitutional and alleging political motives.
articles.body: Thiruvananthapuram: CPM state secretariat on Sunday asked chief minister V D Satheesan to clarify his stand on former governor Rajendra Arlekar’s recommendation to the President to dissolve the Kerala Public Service Commission (PSC).In a statement, CPM termed Arlekar’s move unconstitutional and illegal and questioned whether the Congress supported it. The party also asked whether the chief minister shared the Congress’s national-level position on what it described as politically motivated actions by governors.CPM said there were established legal procedures for taking action against PSC members, but the governor had not followed them. It pointed out that a special investigation team was already probing allegations of irregularities in the preparation of a PSC rank list. The govt had informed the high court that the investigation had found nothing so far, though the court had made certain critical observations, the party said.The party said the governor had no authority to recommend the dissolution of the PSC and was bound to act on the advice of the state govt. It asked whether the govt had requested the governor to make such a recommendation when none of the allegations had been proved or substantiated before a court.Alleging that the Sangh Parivar was targeting PSC after universities in the state, CPM called for strong protests against what it described as “governor’s rule” that reduced democracy to a mere spectator. It said the move would be challenged both politically and legally.The party also demanded that Satheesan clarify whether the govt had handed over any crucial files or information concerning PSC to Arlekar. It alleged that Arlekar had relied solely on complaints and media reports, which were insufficient grounds for such a recommendation.Accusing the state govt of yielding to the Sangh Parivar, CPM referred to the farewell accorded to Arlekar by the govt and the chief minister’s expressions of warmth towards him. It also alleged that several decisions, including the appointment of university vice-chancellors, were part of an understanding involving BJP and RSS.The party said the governor was expected to act on the advice of the state govt but had repeatedly bypassed it, including in the PSC issue.Defending the commission, CPM said Kerala PSC had set an example for the rest of the country by completing recruitment processes quickly. It claimed that the commission had made more than 10 lakh appointments over the past 10 years.The party maintained that isolated incidents should not be used to discredit an entire constitutional institution.
